title: Medical Alert Systems With Fall Detection: A Plain-English Buying Guide
subtitle: How these help buttons work, what the monthly bill really looks like, and what fall detection can and cannot do.
excerpt: A medical alert button can bring help with one press, and some can call for you after a fall. Here is how home and GPS units differ, what they cost each month, and why you should still press the button.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Falls are common as we get older. According to the CDC, more than 14 million adults age 65 and up, about 1 in 4, report falling every year, and falls are the leading cause of injury in that age group. Most falls end with a bruise and a story. The worry is the one that leaves you on the floor, alone, with the phone across the room.

That is the job a medical alert system does. You wear a small button, press it, and a trained agent answers through the device and sends help. Many systems now offer automatic fall detection as well. Here is what to know before you sign up.
How a medical alert system works

Every system has two parts: a device you wear, usually as a pendant, wristband or belt clip, and a monthly monitoring service. When you press the button, the device connects you to a monitoring center. An agent talks with you, and depending on what you need, calls a family member, a neighbor or emergency services.
Home units vs. mobile GPS units

Home systems use a base station that plugs into the wall, connecting over a landline or a cellular signal. They work well if you spend most of your day at home, and they cost a little less. Bay Alarm Medical, for example, lists its SOS Home plan at $27.95 a month on a landline and $34.95 a month on cellular.

Mobile units are small all-in-one devices with a built-in speaker, cellular connection and GPS, so they work at the grocery store, in the garden or on a walk. If you drive, golf or still run your own errands, a mobile unit is usually the better fit. You will need to charge it, often every few days.
What fall detection can and cannot do

Fall detection uses motion sensors in the device. Bay Alarm Medical describes it as looking for a sudden downward movement followed by a lack of movement. When it senses that pattern, it calls the monitoring center for you, which matters most if you are hurt, dizzy or unable to reach the button.

It is a backup, not a guarantee. Lively states plainly that its fall detection does not detect 100% of falls, and Bay Alarm Medical says no automatic fall detection system is 100% accurate. Because the sensor looks for a sudden drop, a slow slide out of a chair may not trigger it, and false alarms can happen too. Bay Alarm Medical's advice is simple:
Always push the button if you're physically able to do so. (Bay Alarm Medical)
Fall detection is usually an add-on of about $10 a month on the plans we looked at. For many people living alone, that is money well spent, as long as everyone understands its limits.
What to look for before you buy

items: Add up the real cost: the monthly fee, any device or equipment charge, the fall detection add-on, and taxes. Some companies sell the device; others include it with the plan.
Ask whether the low monthly price requires paying a year up front. Several of the prices advertised are for annual plans or limited-time promotions.
Check for contracts and cancellation fees. Some services say they have no long-term contract; others note that cancellation fees may apply.
Match the device to your day. Home-only units are simpler; GPS units follow you out the door but need regular charging.
Make sure it is comfortable enough to wear all day, including in the shower. Check whether the maker says it is water resistant.
Ask who can be notified, such as adult children or a neighbor, and whether there is a caregiver app.

sections.label: Good to Know
sections.content: Fall detection is not recommended for everyone. Bay Alarm Medical says its automatic fall detection should not be used by people with memory loss or seizures, and should only be a backup plan. If that describes you or a loved one, talk with the company and your doctor about the best setup.

A medical alert system only helps if you wear it, keep it charged and press it when something feels wrong. Pick the type that fits how you live, home unit or GPS, add fall detection if you live alone or have fallen before, and read the fine print on fees. Then put it on and get on with your day.

products.name: SOS Home (Cellular) with Fall Detection
products.price: About $44.95 a month (list price, October 2026); base unit included, plus a $30 charge for the fall detection button
products.blurb: An in-home base station that runs on a cellular signal, with a fall detection wearable included. A good fit for people who spend most of their time at home and do not have a landline.

products.name: SOS Micro with Fall Detection
products.price: About $44.95 a month plus a device charge of $149 list (shown at $104.30 on sale, October 2026)
products.blurb: A small mobile GPS button that works in and away from home. Suits active people who drive, walk or run errands on their own.

products.name: Lively Mobile2 All-in-One Medical Alert
products.price: About $119.99 for the device (list price; $89.99 on sale, October 2026), plus a Basic plan at $24.99 a month or Premium at $34.99 a month; fall detection adds $9.99 a month
products.blurb: A mobile all-in-one device with no long-term contract, according to Lively. Its lower Basic plan makes it one of the less expensive monthly options, though fall detection is an extra charge.

products.name: Guardian Flex
products.price: About $39.95 a month on the annual plan (October 2026); device lists at $149.95; fall detection add-on: check current price
products.blurb: A mobile GPS device worn as a necklace or on a belt clip, with up to five days of battery life per charge, according to Medical Guardian. Fall detection is an optional add-on.
